procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, set aside the impugned orders of the High Court.

directions: The impugned orders passed by the High Court are hereby set aside.
Prior to carrying out further investigation under Section 173(8) of the CrPC it is not necessary that the order accepting the final report should be reviewed, recalled or quashed.

issue.issue_text: Whether sub-section (8) of Section 173 of the CrPC permits further investigation after the Magistrate has accepted a final report (closure report) under sub-section (2) of Section 173 of the CrPC.

law.fact_text: Section 173(8) of the CrPC was introduced to statutorily affirm the right of the police to conduct further investigation after submitting a final report under Section 173(2).
Upon receiving a final report, a Magistrate has three options: accept the report and close the case, disagree and proceed with the case, or order further investigation under Section 156(3).

application.fact_text: The Court, after reviewing its previous decisions, established that the acceptance of a final (closure) report by a Magistrate does not create a bar to further investigation.

It is permissible for the investigating agency to carry out further investigation under Section 173(8) of the CrPC even after the Magistrate has accepted the final report submitted under Section 173(2).
The Court clarified that it is not necessary for the Magistrate to review, recall, or quash the order accepting the final report before a further investigation can be carried out.
The power of the police to conduct further investigation can also be initiated at the instance of the court.
The Court noted a procedural requirement that the police should seek formal permission from the Court before commencing a further investigation.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that Section 173(8) of the CrPC permits an investigating agency to conduct further investigation even after a Magistrate has accepted a final (closure) report. The acceptance of the report does not terminate the proceedings, and the order accepting it does not need to be reviewed or recalled for further investigation to commence.

issue.issue_text: Whether it is necessary that the order accepting the final report should be reviewed, recalled or quashed prior to carrying out further investigation under Section 173(8) of the CrPC.

law.law_text: Section 173(8) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) statutorily empowers the police (investigating agency) to conduct a 'further investigation' even after a final report has been submitted under Section 173(2).
This power to conduct further investigation exists even after the Magistrate has accepted the final report (closure report).
The acceptance of a final report by a Magistrate is a judicial order.

application.application_text: The Supreme Court analyzed the power granted to the investigating agency under Section 173(8) of the CrPC.
The Court determined that this statutory power is independent and is not barred by the Magistrate's prior acceptance of a final report.

It reasoned that since the investigating agency has a clear right to reopen the investigation, this right is not contingent on undoing the Magistrate's previous judicial order. The provisions of Section 173(8) were enacted to specifically allow for such situations.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that it is not necessary for the order accepting the final report to be reviewed, recalled, or quashed before the investigating agency can carry out a further investigation under Section 173(8) of the CrPC.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Prior to carrying out further investigation under Section 173(8) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, it is not necessary that the order accepting the final report should be reviewed, recalled or quashed.
obiter: Courts must adhere to the basics of judicial discipline and the need for predictability and a certainty in law.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court's order was set aside primarily on the procedural ground that the learned Single Judge departed from established principles of judicial decorum and propriety. When a judge is inclined to take a view contrary to earlier decisions of the same court, the proper course is to refer the matter to a larger bench, not to decide the question independently. This procedural failure was sufficient to overturn the High Court's decision.
legal_tests_applied: Considerations of judicial propriety and decorum require that if a learned Single Judge hearing a matter is inclined to take the view that the earlier decisions of the High Court, whether of a Division Bench or of a Single Judge, need to be reconsidered, he should not embark upon that enquiry sitting as a Single Judge, but should refer the matter to a Division Bench or, in a proper case, place the relevant papers before the Chief Justice to enable him to constitute a larger Bench to examine the question.
why_appellant_lost: The argument that a Magistrate cannot permit further investigation because no matter was pending after the investigation had already been closed was implicitly rejected by the court's final decision to allow the appeal.
why_respondent_won: The High Court's order was procedurally flawed as the learned Single Judge departed from the traditional and proper way of dealing with binding precedent, failing to adhere to principles of judicial decorum and propriety by not referring the matter to a larger bench.
When a court with jurisdiction passes an order for further investigation, it is for the ends of justice, and it would not be a proper exercise of revisional powers to interfere with such an order.
policy_considerations: The proper and traditional way for a judge to handle disagreement with earlier precedent is founded on healthy principles of judicial decorum and propriety, which require referring the question to a larger bench to maintain judicial discipline.
Further investigation under Section 173(8) of the CrPC serves the ends of justice.
